source_text: Οὕτω σε διὰ πάντων ἐγρηγορέναι ὁ κτίστης βούλεται, ἵν' ἐν τῇ πρὸς Θεὸν ἐλπίδι τὰς ἀπ' αὐτῶν βλάβας ἀποδιδράσκῃς. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀνα δραμόντες ἐκ τῶν βυθῶν, ἐπὶ τὴν ἤπειρον καταφύγωμεν. Καὶ γάρ πως ἄλλα ἐπ' ἄλλοις καταλαβόντα ἡμᾶς τῆς δημιουργίας τὰ θαύματα, οἷόν τινα κύματα, ταῖς συνεχέσι καὶ ἐπαλλήλοις ἐπιδρομαῖς ὑποβρόχιον ἡμῶν τὸν λόγον ἤγαγε. Καίτοι θαυμάσαιμι ἂν, εἰ μὴ μείζοσι τοῖς κατ' ἤπειρον παραδόξοις ἡ διάνοια ἡμῶν ἐντυχοῦσα, πάλιν κατὰ τὸν Ἰωνᾶν ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν δραπετεύσει. Ἔοικε δέ μοι ὁ λόγος ἐμπεσὼν εἰς τὰ μυρία θαύματα ἐπιλελῆσθαι τῆς συμμετρίας, καὶ ταὐτὸν πεπονθέναι τοῖς ἐν πελάγει ναυτιλλομένοις, οἳ πρὸς μηδὲν πεπηγὸς τὴν κίνησιν τεκμαιρόμενοι, ἀγνοοῦσι πολλάκις ὅσον διέδραμον. Ὃ δὴ καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς ἔοικε γεγενῆσθαι, τρέχοντος τοῦ λόγου διὰ τῆς κτίσεως, μὴ λαβεῖν τοῦ πλήθους τῶν εἰρημένων τὴν αἴσθησιν. Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ φιλήκοον τὸ σεμνὸν τοῦτο θέατρον, καὶ γλυκεῖα δούλων ἀκοαῖς δεσποτικῶν θαυμάτων διήγησις, ἐνταῦθα τὸν λόγον ὁρμίσαντες, μείνωμεν τὴν ἡμέραν πρὸς τὴν τῶν λειπομένων ἀπόδοσιν. Ἀναστάντες δὲ πάντες εὐχαριστή σωμεν ὑπὲρ τῶν εἰρημένων, καὶ αἰτήσωμεν τῶν λειπομένων τὴν πλήρωσιν. Γένοιτο δὲ ὑμῖν καὶ ἐν τῇ μεταλήψει τῆς τροφῆς ἐπιτραπέζια διηγήματα, ὅσα τε ἕωθεν ὑμῖν, καὶ ὅσα κατὰ τὴν ἑσπέραν ἐπῆλθεν ὁ λόγος· καὶ ταῖς περὶ τούτων ἐννοίαις ὑπὸ τοῦ ὕπνου καταληφθέντες, τῆς μεθημερινῆς εὐφροσύνης καὶ καθεύδοντες ἀπολαύσοιτε, ἵνα ἐξῇ ὑμῖν λέγειν, Ἐγὼ καθεύδω, καὶ ἡ καρδία μου ἀγρυπνεῖ, μελετῶσα νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας ἐν τῷ νόμῳ Κυρίου, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ηʹ Περὶ πτηνῶν καὶ ἐνύδρων. 8.1 Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἐξαγαγέτω ἡ γῆ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν κατὰ γένος, τετράποδα καὶ ἑρπετὰ καὶ θηρία κατὰ γένος. Καὶ ἐγένετο οὕτως. Ἦλθε τὸ πρόσταγμα ὁδῷ βαδίζον, καὶ ἀπέλαβε καὶ ἡ γῆ τὸν ἴδιον κόσμον. Ἐκεῖ, Ἐξαγαγέτω τὰ ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν· ὧδε, Ἐξαγαγέτω ἡ γῆ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν. Ἔμψυχος ἄρα ἡ γῆ; καὶ χώραν ἔχουσιν οἱ ματαιόφρονες Μανιχαῖοι, ψυχὴν ἐντιθέντες τῇ γῇ; Οὐκ ἐπειδὴ εἶπεν, Ἐξαγαγέτω, τὸ ἐναποκείμενον αὐτῇ προήνεγκεν, ἀλλ' ὁ δοὺς τὸ πρόσταγμα, καὶ τὴν τοῦ ἐξαγαγεῖν αὐτῇ δύναμιν ἐχαρίσατο. Οὔτε γὰρ ὅτε ἤκουσεν ἡ γῆ, Βλαστησάτω βοτάνην χόρτου καὶ ξύλον κάρπιμον, κεκρυμμένον ἔχουσα τὸν χόρτον ἐξήνεγκεν· οὐδὲ τὸν φοίνικα, ἢ τὴν δρῦν, ἢ τὴν κυπάρισσον κάτω που ἐν ταῖς λαγόσιν ἑαυτῆς ἀποκε κρυμμένα ἀνῆκε πρὸς τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν· ἀλλ' ὁ θεῖος λόγος φύσις ἐστὶ τῶν γινομένων. Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ· οὐχ ὅπερ ἔχει προβαλλέτω, ἀλλ' ὃ μὴ ἔχει κτησάσθω, Θεοῦ δωρουμένου τῆς ἐνεργείας τὴν δύναμιν. Οὕτω καὶ νῦν, Ἐξαγαγέτω ἡ γῆ ψυχὴν, οὐ τὴν ἐναποκειμένην, ἀλλὰ τὴν δεδομένην αὐτῇ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τῆς ἐπιταγῆς. Ἔπειτα καὶ εἰς τὸ ἐναντίον αὐτοῖς ὁ λόγος περιτραπήσεται. Εἰ γὰρ ἐξήνεγκεν ἡ γῆ τὴν ψυχὴν, ἐρήμην ἑαυτὴν κατέλιπε τῆς ψυχῆς. Ἀλλ' ἐκείνων μὲν τὸ βδελυκτὸν αὐτόθεν γνώριμον. Διὰ τί μέντοι τὰ μὲν ὕδατα ἑρπετὰ ψυχῶν ζωσῶν ἐξαγαγεῖν προσετάχθη, ἡ δὲ γῆ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν; Λογιζόμεθα τοίνυν, ὅτι τῶν μὲν νηκτῶν ἡ φύσις ἀτελεστέρας πως δοκεῖ ζωῆς μετέχειν, διὰ τὸ ἐν τῇ παχύτητι τοῦ ὕδατος διαιτᾶσθαι.
thought_title: The Creator's wonders on land and the transition to land animals
orientation: Basil is closing his homily on sea creatures and beginning the next homily, where he turns to the land animals created on the sixth day.
pass_a_gloss: Thus the Creator wishes you to be awake through all things, so that in hope toward God you may escape the harms from them. But come, having run back up from the depths, let us flee for refuge to the mainland. For indeed the wonders of creation, coming upon us one after another, like some waves, with their continuous and successive onsets, have led our discourse under water. And yet I would be amazed if our mind, encountering the greater marvels on land, would not again flee to the sea like Jonah. But the discourse, having fallen into the countless wonders, seems to me to have forgotten its measure, and to have suffered the same thing as those sailing on the open sea, who, judging their movement by nothing fixed, often do not know how far they have run. This very thing seems to have happened also to us, as the discourse ran through creation, that we did not perceive the multitude of the things said. But even if this august theater loves to hear, and the narration of the Master's wonders is sweet to the ears of servants, having anchored the discourse here, let us remain for the day for the giving of what remains. And having risen, let us all give thanks for the things said, and let us ask for the fulfillment of what remains. And may there be for you also, in the partaking of food, table narratives, as many as came to you in the morning, and as many as the discourse brought in the evening; and being overtaken by sleep with thoughts about these things, may you enjoy the daytime gladness even while sleeping, so that it may be possible for you to say, I sleep, and my heart keeps watch, meditating night and day on the law of the Lord, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages of ages. Amen. Homily 8. On birds and water creatures. 8.1 And God said, Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to kind, four-footed animals and creeping things and wild beasts according to kind. And it became so. The command came walking by a road, and the earth also received its own order. There, Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls; here, Let the earth bring forth a living creature. Is the earth then ensouled? And do the foolish Manichaeans have room, putting a soul into the earth? Not because he said, Let it bring forth, did it bring forward what was stored up in it, but the one who gave the command also granted to it the power of bringing forth. For neither when the earth heard, Let it sprout the herb of grass and the fruit-bearing tree, did it bring out the grass as something it had hidden; nor did it send up to the surface the palm, or the oak, or the cypress hidden somewhere below in its hollows; but the divine word is the nature of the things that come to be. Let the earth sprout: not let it put forward what it has, but let it acquire what it does not have, God granting the power of the activity. So also now, Let the earth bring forth a soul, not the one stored up in it, but the one given to it by God through the command. Then also the argument will be turned around against them to the opposite. For if the earth brought out the soul, it left itself bereft of the soul. But their abomination is known from this very thing. Why, however, were the waters commanded to bring forth creeping things of living souls, but the earth a living creature? We reason, then, that the nature of swimming things seems somehow to share in a more incomplete life, because they pass their life in the thickness of the water.

lemmas.gloss: to be awake, to keep watch
to escape, to run away from
to anchor, to bring to anchor

choices.why: Basil consistently uses this title for God as maker of all things; the brief's argument emphasizes deliberate creation by God.

choices.english: let us flee for refuge to the mainland
choices.why: The verb καταφεύγω means to flee for refuge, not merely to go; Basil frames the move from sea to land as a rhetorical escape from the overwhelming wonders.
rejected: let us take refuge on the land
let us escape to the continent

choices.english: have led our discourse under water
choices.why: The adjective ὑποβρόχιος means submerged or under water; Basil's metaphor is that the successive wonders have drowned or submerged the discourse.
Συμμετρία here means due proportion or proper measure; Basil says the discourse has forgotten its proper limit or proportion.
Σεμνός means august, reverend, solemn; Basil addresses his congregation as a solemn or august audience, a common homiletic address.
The brief's glossary mandates 'living creature' for ψυχὴν ζῶσαν, used for animals as distinct from plants.

pass_b_english: So through all these things the Creator wants you to stay awake, so that by your hope in God you may escape the harm they can do. But let us now run back up from the depths and flee for refuge to the mainland. For the wonders of creation, coming upon us one after another like waves, have led our discourse under water by their continuous and successive assaults. And yet I would be surprised if our mind, once it encounters the greater marvels of the land, does not again run away to the sea like Jonah. It seems to me that our discourse, having fallen among countless wonders, has forgotten its measure, and has suffered the same thing as those who sail on the open sea: with no fixed point by which to judge their movement, they often do not know how far they have traveled. This seems to have happened to us as well: as our discourse ran through creation, we did not perceive the sheer number of things said. But even if this august theater loves to listen, and the telling of the Master's wonders is sweet to the ears of His servants, let us anchor our discourse here and wait for the day to render what remains. And when we all rise, let us give thanks for what has been said, and ask for the completion of what remains. May there also be for you, in the partaking of your food, table-talk about all that came to you this morning and all that our discourse brought this evening. And may you be overtaken by sleep with thoughts about these things, so that even while sleeping you enjoy the daytime's gladness, and may it be possible for you to say, "I sleep, but my heart is awake," meditating night and day on the law of the Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen. Homily 8: On birds and water creatures. 8.1 And God said, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to kind: four-footed animals and creeping things and wild beasts according to kind." And it was so (Genesis 1:24). The command came walking along its path, and the earth received its own adornment. There, "Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living creatures" (Genesis 1:20); here, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature." Is the earth then ensouled? Do the foolish Manichaeans have any ground for putting a soul into the earth? It is not because He said "Let it bring forth" that the earth brought out what was stored up within it; rather, the One who gave the command also granted it the power to bring forth. For when the earth heard, "Let it sprout the herb of grass and the fruit tree" (Genesis 1:11), it did not bring out grass it had hidden within itself; it did not send up to the surface a palm tree or an oak or a cypress that had been stored away somewhere in its hollows. No, the divine word is the nature of the things that come to be. "Let the earth sprout": not "let it cast out what it has," but "let it acquire what it does not have," since God grants the power to be active. So now also, "Let the earth bring forth a living creature": not the one stored up within it, but the one given to it by God through the command. And then the argument will turn back against them in the opposite direction. For if the earth brought out the soul, it left itself bereft of soul. But their abomination is obvious immediately. Why, however, were the waters commanded to bring forth creeping things of living creatures, while the earth was commanded to bring forth a living creature? We reason, then, that the nature of swimming things seems to share in a life that is somehow less complete, because they live in the thickness of the water.

problems.quote: Is the earth then a living thing?
problems.why: Ἔμψυχος means 'ensouled/having a soul', not merely 'living thing'; this misrepresents the philosophical issue
problems.ruling: Ἔμψυχος means 'ensouled'; 'living thing' loses the soul/ψυχή argument central against Manichaeans.

problems.quote: their abomination is obvious from the start
problems.source_quote: ἐκείνων μὲν τὸ βδελυκτὸν αὐτόθεν γνώριμον
problems.why: αὐτόθεν means 'from that very source/therefrom', i.e., 'from that very argument' or 'from that consideration', not 'from the start' temporally
problems.fix: their abomination is obvious from that very argument
problems.ruling: αὐτόθεν means 'from that very thing/argument', not 'from the start'; misleads reader on the logical reference.
